parsed_answer.content:
The self-invocation problem in Spring AOP and declarative transactions (@Transactional) is one of the most insidious architectural traps encountered by Java developers working with the Spring Framework. To understand why it happens, we must examine how Spring implements aspect-oriented programming and transaction management: through dynamic proxies. When a client calls a public method on a Spring bean, it is rarely invoking the raw target instance directly. Instead, Spring wraps the bean in either a JDK dynamic proxy (if implementing interfaces) or a CGLIB subclass proxy (for class-based proxies). This proxy intercepts the method call, invokes any configured interceptors—such as transaction interceptors that start a database session or open a connection—and then delegates the call to the actual target object.

The self-invocation problem occurs when a method within the target bean calls another method on *itself* using the `this` reference. Because `this` points to the raw target object and not the surrounding proxy, the internal method call completely bypasses the proxy infrastructure. Consequently, any cross-cutting concerns attached to the inner method—most notably @Transactional declarative transaction boundaries, security checks, or caching annotations—are entirely ignored. If an inner method throws an exception, the outer caller's transaction manager will not catch it to trigger a rollback, or conversely, a method marked with @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW) will execute within the context of the calling transaction instead of spinning up a new physical transaction, leading to unexpected data consistency bugs.

items: Proxy Bypass Mechanism: The `this` reference inside a Spring bean instance refers to the raw target object, routing execution straight to the target's method table without traversing the `AopProxy` or `MethodInterceptor` chains.

Transaction Interceptor Ignored: Declarative transaction management relies on the `TransactionInterceptor` catching exceptions and handling commits/rollbacks. Self-invocation never hits this interceptor.

Refactoring Solutions: The problem can be resolved either by refactoring the self-invoking method into a separate Spring-managed bean, or by injecting an application context-aware proxy of the current bean using `AopContext.currentProxy()`.

parsed_answer.content: In production, relying on `AopContext.currentProxy()` to fix self-invocation requires setting `@EnableAspectJAutoProxy(exposeProxy = true)` explicitly on your configuration, otherwise it throws an IllegalStateException indicating that no proxy is available. However, heavy reliance on `AopContext` smells like a code smell; the cleaner architectural fix is always to extract the transactional logic into a distinct collaborator service bean.

title: Self-invocation problem in Spring AOP / Transactions
